beginner: Pole beans grow best in rich, loose soil that drains well. Loam, a balanced soil that holds some moisture but never stays soggy, is ideal. Because these vines bear for a long time, they want steady moisture through the season, but wet, waterlogged ground rots the roots. Put your trellis or poles in when you plant so you do not disturb the roots later.
seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam. Pole beans set the heaviest pods in soil that holds moisture through their long pod-fill season yet never stays waterlogged, since soggy ground invites the root rots beans are prone to. Work in compost before planting and set the trellis or poles in place at the same time so you do not disturb the roots later.

beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils work fine as long as they drain well. Sandy soil dries out faster, so you may need to feed a little more often. Heavier soil does better if you mix in compost, which keeps it from crusting over the seedlings as they push up.
seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both work if drainage is good. Sandy beds dry faster and may need a touch more frequent sidedressing; heavier soils benefit from worked-in organic matter to keep them from crusting over the emerging seedlings.

beginner: Stay away from heavy soil that drains poorly, and soil that forms a hard crust after it rains. A crust can trap young seedlings before they reach the surface, and water sitting around the roots can bring on the root rot that beans catch easily.
seasoned: Avoid heavy, poorly drained ground and soils that crust hard after rain. A crust can trap the seedling below the surface, and standing water around the roots brings on the root-rot diseases beans are prone to.

beginner: Pole beans like loose, fertile soil that drains well. If water sits on top of your bed for a long time after rain, work in some compost first to help it drain.
seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam, ideally with compost worked in before planting. The critical trait is steady moisture without waterlogging through the long pod-set and pod-fill season.

beginner: Pole beans do well in slightly acidic to neutral soil. If you have not tested your soil, a pH near 6.5 is a safe target and most garden beds are already close.
seasoned: A soil pH of 5.8 to 6.5 suits snap beans; they tolerate up to about neutral. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

beginner: Pole beans make a lot of their own food from the air, so they need little fertilizer. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant, and feed once more lightly right before the plants flower. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines climbing the trellis but fewer beans, and it delays flowering.
seasoned: Pole beans are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, and excess nitrogen delays flowering and pushes leafy vine growth up the trellis at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a balanced starter into the bed before planting, then sidedress lightly just before the first bloom. Sandy beds or leaching rains can call for a second light feeding across the long bearing season.

beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 works well.
seasoned: Pre-plant 5-10-10 if no soil test is available; sidedress a nitrogen source lightly before bloom.

beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet of bed before planting.
seasoned: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, per Clemson HGIC.

beginner: Pole beans get along with most vegetables. The classic combination is beans, corn, and squash grown together, with the beans climbing the corn. The one pairing to avoid is planting beans right next to onions or garlic.
seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, pole beans leave the soil better for what follows and are the classic climbing partner in the Three Sisters planting, where the beans scramble up the corn while squash covers the ground. The long-standing caution is to keep beans away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress them.

beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; with pole beans the corn works as a living pole for the vines to climb.
seasoned: Corn is the classic pole bean partner in Three Sisters planting, where the corn stalk serves as a living trellis for the climbing vines. Let the corn get a good head start and use sturdy, well-rooted stalks, since vigorous pole beans can overload thin sweet corn. The beans' nitrogen fixation helps balance the bed for the heavy-feeding corn; the benefit is structural and traditional rather than a measured pest effect.

beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the beans.
seasoned: Squash rounds out the Three Sisters trio. Its broad sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the base of the bean supports, while the mix of heights makes it harder for pests to lock onto any one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp the young bean vines before they climb.

beginner: An easy neighbor that shares similar warm-season, full-sun needs.
seasoned: Cucumber and pole beans coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing and water needs, and the beans' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. Trellised cucumbers can even share the vertical structure. This is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one.

beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans, which are said to grow poorly near them.
seasoned: Onions and beans is one of the better-grounded 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, the very bacteria the bean depends on to fix nitrogen, so bean growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. A useful corollary: beans grown before onions actually improve the soil for the following allium crop.

beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans.
seasoned: Garlic acts on beans the same way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, slowing the beans down. Treat garlic and pole beans as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the bean-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

beginner: Leaves that look skeletonized or lacy, with the tissue chewed away from underneath but the veins left behind. Both the spiny yellow young and the round, coppery adult beetles feed on the undersides of the leaves, and on a tall pole vine they work their way up high where they are easy to overlook. The adult is yellow to copper colored with rows of small black spots on its back.
seasoned: Leaves taking on a skeletonized, lacy look as tissue is chewed from the undersides, leaving the vein network behind. Both the spiny yellow larvae and the dome-shaped, coppery adults feed on leaf undersides, and on tall pole vines the damage runs high into the canopy where it is easy to miss. The adult is yellow to coppery-brown, one-quarter to one-third inch long, with eight small black spots on each wing cover.

beginner: The Mexican bean beetle, a leaf-eating cousin of the ladybug. The adults come out of hiding near woods in spring, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves, and several generations build up over the summer.
seasoned: The Mexican bean beetle (Epilachna varivestis), a leaf-eating member of the ladybeetle family. Adults emerge from overwintering near woodland edges, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides, and several generations build through the season.

beginner: Pick off and destroy the adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny young, looking under the leaves and up the vine. Done early, this works well in a home garden. Beans can lose a fair amount of leaf without losing beans, so you do not need to spray for light damage. If they get bad, an organic spray such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles.
seasoned: Handpick and destroy adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny larvae, checking leaf undersides up the trellis. Beans tolerate real defoliation without yield loss, about 30 percent before bloom and 15 percent during bloom and pod fill, so light feeding needs no spray. Where pressure is heavy, an organic option such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles.

beginner: Because most damage happens in July and August, planting early or making a late-summer sowing can mostly dodge it. Clear and turn under the old vines right after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your beans to a new spot each year.
seasoned: Since most damage falls in July and August, an early or a late-summer sowing can escape the worst of it; the varieties Wade and Black Valentine are noted as tolerant. Work crop debris into the soil promptly after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate beans away from last year's bed.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, usually green but sometimes black or pink, packed onto the growing tips and the undersides of leaves. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and slows them down, and a sticky residue may appear. Aphids can also spread virus diseases from plant to plant.
seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied, pinhead-sized insects clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, usually green but sometimes black, yellow, or pink. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and delays maturity as the insects withdraw sap; sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow.

beginner: Several kinds of aphids, most common in cool, dry weather on small plants. They multiply fast and build up thick colonies before their natural enemies catch up. Warmer weather and helpful bugs like ladybugs usually knock them back.
seasoned: Several aphid species (Aphis and Macrosiphum euphorbiae), most prevalent in cool, dry weather on small plants. They reproduce rapidly, building dense colonies before natural enemies catch up; warm weather and predators such as ladybugs usually bring them down.

beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them. Once it warms up, ladybugs and other helpful insects usually take care of the rest.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which gives good control on contact. Begin as soon as colonies are found. Once the weather warms, ladybugs and other natural enemies generally take over.

beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts both their feeding and the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like.
seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor.

beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves at first, turning to a dried, bronzed look as they multiply. The clue is fine webbing on the undersides of the leaves. The mites themselves are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
seasoned: A fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves at first, progressing to a bronzed, dried-out look as populations build; fine silken webbing over the leaf undersides is the giveaway. The mites are minute specks, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather.

beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry weather lets them build up fast, and dusty, dried-out plants are the most likely to be hit.
seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry conditions favor rapid buildup, and dusty, drought-stressed plants are most prone.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get too thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down.
seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap before numbers climb too high. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and ladybugs and other predators help.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.
seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and avoid the dusty conditions mites thrive in. Watch the undersides of leaves closely through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.

beginner: Large ragged holes chewed in the leaves, and on young plants, chewing around the stem near the soil that can kill seedlings. The adult is a small beetle, usually reddish or yellowish, with a few black spots down each wing cover. Early-season damage is the worst because it thins out the plants.
seasoned: Large, irregular holes chewed in leaves, and on young plants, girdling of stems near the soil line that can thin the stand. The adult is one-fifth to one-quarter inch long and variable in color, usually red to yellow, marked with three or four black spots along each wing cover. Damage early in the season matters most because it reduces the stand.

beginner: The bean leaf beetle, which is rarely a serious problem in most home gardens. The adults chew leaves and stems, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), rarely a serious pest in most home gardens. Adults feed on foliage and stems, with seedlings the most vulnerable stage.

beginner: Picking them off and the same steps you would use for Mexican bean beetle usually keep them in check. Beans can lose a good bit of leaf without losing beans, so light damage needs nothing. Focus on protecting young seedlings, which are the most at risk.
seasoned: Handpicking and the same measures used against Mexican bean beetle generally keep it in check; beans tolerate considerable leaf loss without yield penalty, so light feeding needs no action. Protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, where beetles are active.

beginner: Clear away the old vines after harvest and move your beans each year so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter. A lightweight row cover over young seedlings protects them through the risky early weeks if this beetle is a problem where you are.
seasoned: Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate beans to deny overwintering sites. A floating row cover over emerging seedlings protects the stand through the vulnerable early weeks where the beetle is a known problem.

beginner: Rust-colored bumps, mostly on the undersides of the leaves. Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wilt, and fall off. Stems and pods can get it too. It shows up in humid weather and can hit most kinds of beans.
seasoned: Rust-colored, raised spots that form mainly on the lower leaf surfaces; badly infected leaves yellow, wilt, and drop. Stems and pods can be infected too. It develops under humid conditions and can affect most types of beans.

beginner: A fungus that survives the winter in the soil, on old plant debris, and, importantly for pole beans, on the poles and trellis used the year before. Humid weather is what lets it take hold and spread.
seasoned: The fungus Uromyces appendiculatus. It survives the winter in the soil, on plant debris, and, importantly for pole beans, on the poles and trellis used the previous year, a direct route back to a new crop. Humid conditions drive infection and spread.

beginner: Pick off and throw away, do not compost, infected leaves, and give the vines room to breathe. Where rust is bad, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control if you start as the plants begin to flower and repeat every week or two, following the label.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves and improve airflow. Where rust has been severe, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control when begun as the plants start to bloom and repeated on a 10-to-14-day schedule; follow the label.

beginner: Move your beans to a new spot if rust has been a problem, and clean or replace your poles and trellis between years, since the fungus rides over on them. Water at the base instead of overhead, keep airflow up, and pick a rust-resistant variety if it keeps coming back.
seasoned: Rotate beans where rust has been a problem, and because the fungus carries over on poles and trellis, clean or replace supports between seasons rather than reusing them unwashed. Grow on a support with good airflow, avoid overhead watering, and choose rust-resistant varieties where it recurs.

beginner: Black, sunken spots about half an inch across on the pods, the clearest sign, sometimes with a pinkish ooze in wet weather. The veins on the undersides of leaves turn black, and spots show up on stems too. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
seasoned: Black, sunken lesions about half an inch across on pods, the most prominent sign, sometimes oozing salmon-colored spores in wet weather; the veins on lower leaf surfaces turn black, and lesions appear on stems and seedling leaves. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.

beginner: A fungus that rides in on infected seed and survives up to two years on old plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum lindemuthianum, carried on infected seed and surviving up to two years on plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet conditions favor infection.

beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away, do not compost, affected plants and debris to slow it down. On snap beans a copper fungicide can help if you start early, but keeping seed clean and rotating does most of the work.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and debris to limit spread. On snap beans a copper fungicide or chlorothalonil can suppress it when started early, but clean seed and rotation do most of the work.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old plants after harvest, and do not grow beans in that spot for two to three years. Water at the base and avoid splashing soil up onto the plants.
seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all plant debris after harvest, and do not plant beans where the disease occurred for two to three years. Avoid overhead watering and splashing soil onto the plants.

beginner: Two related diseases. Halo blight makes pale greenish-yellow rings around brown spots on the leaves and shows up in cool weather. Common blight turns leaves brown so they drop fast, with no ring, and likes warm weather. Both hit stems, leaves, and pods, and both spread in rain and damp conditions.
seasoned: Two related diseases. Halo blight shows light greenish-yellow halos around brown leaf spots and appears in cool weather; common blight turns leaves brown so they drop quickly, with no halo, and favors warm weather. Both infect stems, leaves, and pods, and both are spread by rain and damp conditions.

beginner: Two kinds of bacteria, one causing common blight and one causing halo blight. Both start on infected seed, spread easily when it is wet, and survive up to two years on old plant debris in the soil.
seasoned: Two bacteria, Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli (common blight) and Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (halo blight). Both start on infected seed, spread readily in moisture, and survive up to two years on plant debris in the soil.

beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper sprays every 10 days can slow it down. Water at the base, not overhead, and do not touch the vines when the leaves are wet, since that carries the bacteria from plant to plant.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper fungicides applied on a 10-day schedule can slow spread. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle the vines when foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.

beginner: Buy new, certified seed each year instead of saving your own, since the disease travels on seed. Do not grow beans in the same spot more than once every three years, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.
seasoned: Buy new, certified seed each year rather than saving it, since the disease is seedborne. Do not plant beans in the same spot more often than every third year, and stay out of the planting when the foliage is wet.

beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a soft, watery rot at the soil line. The roots die and the leaves turn yellow. It is worst in cool, wet soil that makes the seeds sit too long before sprouting.
seasoned: Seeds that rot before emerging, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a watery soft rot just above or below the soil line; roots die and leaves yellow. The damage shows up most in cool, wet soils that slow germination and keep seedlings vulnerable.

beginner: Several fungi that live in the soil and infect seeds and young seedlings, usually Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and damage to the roots at planting are what let them in.
seasoned: Several soilborne fungi that infect seeds and young seedlings, usually Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium species, and Fusarium solani. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and root injury at planting set the stage for them.

beginner: There is no saving seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage limits the loss. The main thing is prevention, since these fungi are already in the soil.
seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss. The real lever is prevention, since the fungi are already in the soil.

beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F before planting, and use raised beds in well-drained ground instead of low, wet spots. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your beans around the garden each year, and clear away old plants after harvest.
seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, and plant on raised beds in well-drained ground rather than low, wet spots. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate beans with other vegetables, and clear crop debris after harvest.

beginner: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that grow fast in cool, damp weather, join together, and choke off the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered in white cottony mold. Crowded, overfed vines with poor airflow are the most at risk.
seasoned: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that enlarge fast under cool, moist conditions, run together, and girdle the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered by a white cottony fungal growth. Dense, overfed vines with poor airflow are most at risk.

beginner: A fungus that thrives in cool, damp weather and heavy, crowded growth. Too much fertilizer makes the lush, dense vines that trap the still, humid air the mold needs.
seasoned: The fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, favored by cool, moist conditions and heavy, dense growth. Too much fertilizer drives the lush vine growth that creates the still, humid canopy the disease needs.

beginner: There is no home-garden spray for this one; you manage it by how you grow. Pull and throw away, do not compost, infected plants, and open up the airflow. Training the vines up their support and thinning crowded growth helps the leaves dry out faster.
seasoned: There is no recommended chemical control for the home garden; management is cultural. Remove and destroy infected plants, and improve air circulation. Training vines up a support and thinning crowded growth helps the canopy dry.

beginner: Give the vines room for air to move instead of crowding them, and go easy on fertilizer, since too much makes the heavy growth the mold likes. Growing up a trellis actually helps, keeping the leaves off the wet ground. Water at the base and avoid keeping the plants wet and packed together.
seasoned: Give plants good airflow rather than crowding, and go easy on fertilizer, since excess nitrogen feeds the heavy vine growth that favors the disease. Vertical growth on a trellis is an advantage here, keeping the canopy off the ground; avoid overhead watering and the wet, still conditions the fungus needs.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist but never soggy. Pole beans flower and fill pods for a long time, so keep the water steady all the way through the season.
seasoned: Regular and even through the long season, keeping soil moisture near field capacity. The need is greatest during the extended flowering and pod-fill period, which on pole beans runs for many weeks.

beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds a deeper root system than frequent light sprinkles.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning. Because pole beans grow up in the air, the leaves dry off faster than on a low bush, which helps keep disease down.
seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so foliage dries quickly; trained up a trellis, the canopy dries faster than a sprawling bush, which helps limit the foliar diseases beans are prone to.

beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots the roots.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted growth point to waterlogged roots and the onset of root rot.

beginner: If plants dry out while flowering and filling pods, they drop their flowers and the beans come out small and tough. Keep the water steady to keep new pods coming.
seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod fill aborts blossoms and produces small, stringy pods, and it can stall the plant's ongoing pod set for the rest of the season.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Bean seeds rot in cold, wet ground.
seasoned: Direct-sown into warm soil, pole beans want an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not soggy: bean seed rots in cold, waterlogged ground.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going and start to climb.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture as they root out and start to climb.

beginner: Water deeply to soak about 6 inches down, in the morning at the soil. Because pole beans climb, the leaves dry off faster than on a low bush, which keeps disease down.
seasoned: Keep soil moisture near field capacity, watering deeply to wet the root zone about 6 inches down, at soil level in the morning. Trained up a trellis the canopy dries fast, which helps limit foliar disease.

beginner: Keep the water steady once the beans flower. On pole beans this is the start of a long season, and drought now can stall pod-setting for weeks.
seasoned: Flowering is moisture-critical, and on pole beans it starts a long run: stress here aborts blossoms and can stall the plant's ongoing pod set for the rest of the season.

beginner: Pole beans flower and fill pods for most of the season, so keep the water steady the whole time, not just once. A dry spell in the middle stalls the running crop.
seasoned: The moisture-critical pod-set-through-pod-fill period on pole beans runs for many weeks of continuous cropping, so keep the water steady all season, not just for one flush. A dry spell mid-run both strings the current pods and stalls the next set.

beginner: Keep watering evenly through the long harvest. Pole beans keep making new pods for weeks, so steady water keeps them coming.
seasoned: Keep even moisture right through the long picking run: pole beans keep setting and filling new pods for weeks as you harvest, and steady water sustains that running yield.

beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is the long stretch when pods are forming and filling.
seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the moisture-critical window is the long pod-set-through-pod-fill period.

seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages, and on pole beans they run for weeks; stress here directly cuts the running yield.

beginner: You do not need to harden off pole beans. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
seasoned: Not applicable. Pole beans are direct-sown in place and are not started indoors or hardened off.

beginner: Plant pole bean seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed and frost is past, and put up the trellis or poles at the same time. Beans do not like having their roots disturbed, so skip starting them indoors.
seasoned: Sow directly into warm soil after the last spring frost, and set the trellis, poles, or netting in place at planting so you do not disturb the roots later. Beans resent root disturbance and germinate quickly in place, so transplanting offers no advantage.

beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers.

beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility; beans need little added nitrogen.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, especially once the vine is large, so check the soil daily in hot weather and water when the top inch is dry.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds, and a full pole vine transpires heavily, so monitor daily in heat and water when the top inch dries.

beginner: Container pole beans still need little feeding; a light dose before flowering, and maybe one more later in the season, is plenty.
seasoned: Feeding needs stay low; a single light pre-bloom feed suffices, though a long-bearing potted vine may want one more light feeding mid-season.

seasoned: Not applicable. As a frost-tender annual, pole beans complete their cycle in a single season and are not overwintered.

beginner: Pole beans can grow in a big pot, but they need a tall, sturdy support they will not tip over. Use a pot at least 5 gallons, ideally 10 or more and 12 inches deep, set up a 6-foot teepee or trellis in it, plant a few seeds around the base, and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Pole beans grow in a large container, but they need both room and a sturdy tall support. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons, ideally 10 or more and 12 inches deep, anchored so a 6-foot teepee or trellis will not topple in wind. Plant several seeds around the support and keep the mix evenly moist.

seasoned: A self-watering container suits pole beans well, smoothing out the steady moisture they want across their long bearing season.

beginner: For pole beans, a deep, heavy pot works better than a wide, shallow one. The pot has to hold up a tall support without tipping in the wind and carry a big vine all season, so depth and weight matter more than width.
seasoned: A deep, heavy, stable container is what matters for pole beans, unlike the wide, shallow pot that suits bush types. The pot has to anchor a 6-foot support against wind and hold enough soil to carry a large vine through a long season, so depth and weight beat surface area here.

beginner: Do not plant beans in the same spot two years running. Diseases build up in the soil and can hit the next bean crop, and they also ride over on old poles and trellis, so clean or replace those too.
seasoned: Avoid following beans with beans or other legumes in the same bed; rotate to break the soil-borne disease cycle beans are prone to. Because rust and blights carry over on poles and trellis, clean or replace those supports between seasons as well as moving the bed.

beginner: Move your beans to a new spot each year, on about a three-year rotation, and clean or swap out the poles and trellis between seasons. Because beans feed the soil with nitrogen, whatever you plant there next will benefit.
seasoned: Rotate beans on a roughly three-year cycle, and clean or replace poles and trellis between seasons since rust and blights persist on them. Their nitrogen-fixing habit makes beans a good predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.

beginner: Do not leave fresh beans out on the counter. They go downhill quickly, so cool them down soon after picking.
seasoned: Not recommended. Fresh snap beans lose quality fast at room temperature and should be cooled promptly after picking rather than held on the counter.

beginner: Cool the beans soon after picking, then keep them in the fridge, cold and a bit humid. They stay good for about a week; left longer or warmer, they get soft spots and brown patches.
seasoned: Cool beans soon after harvest to shed field heat, then refrigerate cold and humid. They hold good quality for about a week; held longer or warmer, they develop watersoaked spots and browning.

beginner: Beans freeze well for keeping longer. For the best result, freeze them within a few hours of picking, after a quick blanch in boiling water to hold their color and texture.
seasoned: Beans freeze well for longer storage. For best quality, freeze or can within a few hours of picking, blanching briefly first to preserve color and texture.

beginner: Snap beans are best eaten soon after picking. To keep them, the trick is to cool them fast and keep them cold: chill them right after harvest, store them cold and damp, and freeze or can them within a few hours if you want the best quality.
seasoned: Snap beans are best used as soon as possible after picking. The key to holding them is speed and cold: cool them right away to remove field heat, keep them cold and humid, and process for the freezer or canner within hours of harvest for top quality.

beginner: Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake Pole are easy, dependable choices for a first pole bean patch. Rattlesnake is a good pick if your summers are hot. One to know: Scarlet Runner bean, with its bright red flowers, is a different plant (Phaseolus coccineus) usually grown for looks, not the same as a snap bean.
seasoned: Choose cultivars with resistance to bean common mosaic virus and anthracnose where those diseases are a concern. The varieties here are widely recommended pole types; Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake Pole lead for dependable, long-bearing crops. Note that Scarlet Runner bean is a different species (Phaseolus coccineus), often grown as an ornamental, not a green-podded snap bean.

beginner: Bare soil for about a week, then a bent stem pushes up through the surface, pulling two thick first leaves (called seed leaves) up with it. Beans come up fast in warm soil but rot in cold, wet ground. If you plant before the soil has warmed to about 60°F, many seeds will not come up at all.
seasoned: Bare soil for roughly a week, then the seedling shoulders up through the surface still bent in a hook, dragging the two thick seed leaves (cotyledons) up with it before they unfold. Emergence is fast in warm soil but stalls or rots outright in cold, wet ground. Beans sown before the soil reaches about 60°F at a 4-inch depth germinate poorly.

beginner: Wait to plant until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil, and put up your trellis or poles at the same time so you do not disturb the roots later. Do not keep the bed soggy.
seasoned: Sow only once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth, about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed, and set the trellis, poles, or netting in place now so you do not disturb the roots later. Avoid soaking the soil, which suffocates the seed and feeds root rot fungi.

beginner: Have your beans come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.
seasoned: Have your beans emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.

beginner: The two seed leaves open, then the real leaves appear, first a single pair, then the three-leaflet leaves beans are known for. The little plant soon starts to reach and twist toward its support. This young stage is when beetles can do the most damage.
seasoned: The cotyledons open and the first true leaves appear: a pair of single leaflets, followed by the bean's characteristic three-part (trifoliate) leaves. The plant soon begins to reach and twine toward its support. Young seedlings are the stage most vulnerable to bean leaf beetle feeding.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, hoeing shallowly since bean roots are near the surface. Check that the trellis or poles are ready and gently steer the first shoots onto them. You do not thin pole beans, they are planted where they will grow.
seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free; young beans compete poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly, since bean roots run close to the surface. Make sure the support is in place and guide the first shoots to it if needed. There is no thinning: pole beans are sown at their spacing along the support.

beginner: How do your young bean plants look? Note any chewed leaves or bare patches.
seasoned: How is your bean stand looking? Note any gaps or beetle damage on the young leaves.

beginner: Fast climbing growth as the vine winds its way up the trellis or poles, often to 6 feet or taller. Pole beans put a lot of early effort into climbing before they make many beans, so at first you will see lots of leafy vine going up rather than pods. Beans make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage.
seasoned: Rapid vining as the plant twines up its support toward its full height, often 6 feet or more. Pole beans spend real energy climbing before they set heavily, so early growth looks leafy and upward rather than fruitful. The plant is fixing much of its own nitrogen now, so vigorous but not lush, overfed growth is the goal.

beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Beans need very little, and extra just gives you big leafy vines and later beans. Tuck any stray shoots onto the support; the vines climb on their own, but a little help early gets them going.
seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture and resist the urge to feed. Beans need little nitrogen, and excess now drives leafy vine growth and delays flowering. Guide wayward shoots onto the support; the vines twine on their own but a nudge helps them find the structure early.

beginner: How tall are your bean vines getting? Note how far up the support they have climbed.
seasoned: How high are your vines climbing? Note their height and how well they are taking to the support.

beginner: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open along the vines. Unlike bush beans, pole beans flower a little at a time over a long stretch, so flowers and young pods appear together for weeks. seasoned: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open along the vines. Pole beans flower over a long, extended window rather than all at once, so bloom and pod set overlap and continue for weeks. This is a moisture-critical stage: water stress aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop until the weather cools.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous, because dry soil now means fewer beans. Water the soil, not the leaves, to keep disease down. If a heat wave hits, water deeply beforehand, then wait it out, the vine will keep flowering once it cools.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample; water stress now directly cuts the running yield. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the tall canopy dry. In a heat wave, water deeply ahead of it; the vine will keep reflowering as temperatures ease.

beginner: Are your beans flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.
seasoned: Are your beans flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.

beginner: Pods form where the flowers were and grow quickly, getting plumper as the beans fill inside. Because the vine keeps flowering, you will have pods of every size at once, from tiny to ready. Dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked pods and can slow down the whole run.
seasoned: Pods appear where flowers were and lengthen quickly, plumping as the seeds fill. Because the vine flowers continuously, you will see pods at every stage at once, from tiny to pickable. Drought here produces small, stringy pods and can stall the plant's ongoing set.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist all through this stage, which on pole beans lasts a long time. Start checking the pods every couple of days, because each one is ready for only a short time before it gets too old.
seasoned: Maintain even moisture near field capacity right through pod fill; on pole beans this stage runs for weeks. Begin checking pods every couple of days as they size up, since the pickable window for any one pod is brief.

beginner: Are pods forming? Note when you first saw them and how quickly they are growing.
seasoned: Are pods forming and filling? Note the date you first saw pods and how fast they are sizing up.

beginner: Firm, crisp pods that break with a clean snap, picked before you can see the seeds bulging. Most pole beans give their first pick around 60 to 70 days and then keep producing for weeks. Picking every couple of days keeps new beans coming; leaving old pods on tells the vine to slow down.
seasoned: Firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly when bent, picked before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod wall. Most pole varieties reach first pick around 60 to 70 days and then keep bearing for many weeks. Regular picking every couple of days keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods; pods left to mature signal it to slow down.

beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, after the dew dries, snapping pods off without tearing the vine. Pick every two or three days all season long, because picking often is what keeps a pole bean producing. Do not pick when the leaves are wet, since that spreads disease.
seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, once the dew has dried, breaking pods off cleanly without tearing the vine. Harvest every two to three days across the whole season; frequent picking is the single biggest lever on how long and heavily a pole bean bears. Do not work the vines when foliage is wet, which spreads bacterial blight.

beginner: Have you picked your first beans? Note the date and keep track of each picking through the season.
seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the date and keep noting each pick to track how long the vines bear.

beginner: Bean seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, because planting early just leads to rotted seed and missing plants. Beans planted into warm soil catch up fast, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
seasoned: Bean seed rots in cold, wet ground. Wait until the soil is at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, since early planting only invites poor stands and seed rot. Beans sown into warm soil quickly overtake those sown into cold soil.

beginner: Put your trellis, teepee, or netting up when you plant, not later. Pole beans climb by themselves but need a strong support, about 6 to 8 feet tall, ready and waiting. Adding it later disturbs the shallow roots.
seasoned: Set the trellis, teepee, or netting in place at sowing, not after the vines are up. Pole beans twine on their own but need a sturdy 6-to-8-foot support ready to climb, and installing it later disturbs shallow bean roots.

beginner: Pull weeds early, but weed shallowly. Young beans do not compete well with weeds, yet their roots are near the surface, so digging deep hurts the plant more than the weeds do. Pull by hand and hoe lightly near the row.
seasoned: Weed early and cultivate shallowly. Young beans compete poorly with weeds, but their roots run close to the surface, so deep hoeing does more harm than the weeds. Hand-pull and scuffle-hoe lightly near the row.

beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Beans make much of their own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy vines and later beans. At most, feed once lightly right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor.
seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy vine growth up the trellis and delays flowering. At most a single light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil.

beginner: Help the young vines find their support early. Pole beans wind their way up on their own, but steering them onto the trellis or pole in the first weeks keeps them from tangling on the ground.
seasoned: Guide the young shoots onto their support early. Pole beans twine counterclockwise on their own, but a nudge onto the trellis or pole in the first weeks keeps them from tangling on the ground and starts the climb clean.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the vine flowers. Flowering and pod-forming are when beans most need water, and on pole beans that lasts a long time, so letting them dry out shrinks the crop. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod set are the moisture-critical stages, and on pole beans they run for weeks, so water stress at any point cuts the running crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead.

beginner: When it stays hotter than about 90°F, beans drop their flowers. The vine gives up on flowers when it is too hot to make beans, then starts again once it cools. Since pole beans flower for a long time, the crop bounces back. Water deeply before a heat wave.
seasoned: Expect blossom drop in sustained heat above about 90°F. The vine aborts flowers when it is too hot to set pods, then resumes once it cools. Because pole beans flower over a long window, the crop recovers as the weather eases; water deeply ahead of a heat wave.

beginner: Do not let the soil dry out while the pods are growing. Dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked beans and can slow the whole run, while steady moisture gives you plump, well-shaped ones all season.
seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out as pods size up. Drought during pod fill produces small, stringy pods and can stall the vine's ongoing set, while steady moisture near field capacity gives plump, well-formed ones over the whole long season.

beginner: Pick every two or three days, before the seeds swell the pods. On pole beans, picking often is what keeps them producing: it keeps new flowers and pods coming, while old pods left on tell the vine to quit. One planting, well picked, keeps going for weeks.
seasoned: Pick every two to three days, before the seeds bulge the pod. On pole beans, frequent picking is the single biggest lever on yield: it keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods, while pods left to mature signal it to slow down. One well-picked planting bears for many weeks.

beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, but wait until the dew has dried off the vines. Touching wet bean plants spreads disease through your patch, so let the leaves dry before you start picking.
seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, but only once the dew has dried. Handling wet bean vines spreads bacterial blight through the planting, so wait for the foliage to dry before working down the rows.

beginner: Pole beans give more from the same patch than bush beans because they grow up instead of out and keep bearing for a long time. A 10-foot row of pole beans usually gives about 8 to 12 pounds of beans over the season, versus around 5 pounds for bush beans in the same space.
seasoned: Pole beans out-yield bush beans from the same footprint by growing vertically and bearing over a long season. A 10-foot row of pole beans typically returns roughly 8 to 12 pounds of pods over its extended cropping period, compared with about 5 pounds for bush beans in the same space.

beginner: Instead of one big batch, pole beans give a steady supply over many weeks from a single planting, all the way to frost. That is why you do not need to replant every couple of weeks like with bush beans: one planting keeps going, as long as you pick every few days.
seasoned: Rather than a single burst, pole beans bear steadily over many weeks from one planting, right up to frost. That long, running harvest is why succession sowing is unnecessary: one well-tended planting keeps a household supplied, provided you pick every couple of days to keep it flowering.

beginner: Pole beans are a satisfying crop for a first-year garden. They come up fast, need little fuss, and one planting keeps making beans for weeks once it starts, about 60 to 70 days from planting. The main things that affect how much you get are keeping the water steady and picking often so the vine keeps producing.
seasoned: Pole beans are a rewarding first-year crop: they germinate quickly, ask little, and a single planting bears for weeks once it starts, around 60 to 70 days from sowing. The main first-year lever on yield is steady moisture through the long flowering and pod-fill season, plus picking often enough to keep the vine producing.

beginner: Flowers fell off without making beans
seasoned: Flowers dropped without setting pods

beginner: The vine flowered, but the flowers fell off without making beans, because steady heat above about 90°F stops the flowers from being pollinated and the plant drops them. Letting the plants dry out while flowering does the same thing. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and since pole beans keep flowering for a long time, the vine usually starts setting beans again once it cools.
seasoned: The vine flowered but the blossoms dropped instead of setting pods, because sustained heat above about 90°F interferes with pollination and the plant aborts flowers it cannot fill. Water stress during bloom has the same effect. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and because pole beans flower over a long window, the vine usually resumes setting pods once temperatures cool.

beginner: Plan your planting so the main flowering skips the hottest part of summer, either early enough to get going before peak heat or, in hot areas, as separate spring and fall plantings around the summer break. Keep the water steady, water deeply before a heat wave, and pick a more heat-tolerant variety like Rattlesnake if your summers are very hot.
seasoned: Time the planting so the heaviest bloom misses the hottest part of summer, sowing early enough to establish before peak heat or, in hot regions, running separate spring and fall sowings around the summer wall. Keep moisture steady, water deeply ahead of a heat wave, and choose more heat-tolerant varieties such as Rattlesnake where summers are reliably hot.

seasoned: The seeds were sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat without germinating and rotted, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Bean seed does not germinate well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start invites soilborne root rot fungi and seedcorn maggot, both of which attack the lingering seed.

beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, since there is no reward for planting beans early. Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after planting.

beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, pole beans is a two-season crop. Plant Mar 1 - Mar 31 for a spring harvest, then plant again Sep 1 - Sep 15 for a fall crop. Skip the hottest stretch of summer: the flowers drop in the worst heat before they can set fruit, so there is nothing to gain by planting through it. It rarely if ever frosts here, so both the spring and fall windows run on Valley heat, not on a frost date.
seasoned: Pole beans in the RGV runs on the Valley's two-crop calendar: set out Mar 1 - Mar 31 for a spring harvest running Apr 20 - Jun 19, then set out again Sep 1 - Sep 15 for a fall harvest running Oct 21 - Dec 4. Sustained heat above the mid-90s°F makes bean blossoms drop before they set pods, so production stops in the hottest weeks even though the vines keep growing. Frost is essentially absent here, so both plantings are timed against heat, not cold. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

beginner: West of the Cascades, pole beans reward a little patience with a long harvest. Put up a sturdy trellis or teepee and sow once the soil has warmed after the last spring frost: May into June on the immediate coast, May into July in the milder Willamette Valley and Puget lowlands. Unlike bush beans, you plant once, not every couple of weeks; the vines then climb and keep setting pods until the first fall frost ends the season. Pick every few days to keep them coming.
seasoned: Pole beans direct-sow at the base of a trellis once the soil has warmed after the last frost. OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table gives the coast (Region 1) a narrower May-to-June window and the Willamette Valley (Region 2) a longer May-to-July window, the same coast-versus-valley pattern seen across the region's warm-season crops. A single planting is enough: the vines bear progressively rather than needing succession sowing, with the earliest pods ready in roughly 60 to 70 days. As a frost-tender crop, harvest continues until the first fall frost, so pick every couple of days through the full stretch.

beginner: Pole beans are the climbing kind of green bean. Instead of staying short like bush beans, they grow as long vines that need something tall to climb, like a trellis, a teepee of poles, or a fence about 6 to 8 feet high. The reward is a long harvest: one planting keeps making beans for weeks, all the way until frost, so you pick a handful every few days instead of getting them all at once. You plant the seeds straight in the garden after the last frost, give them their support, keep them watered, and start picking in about two months.
seasoned: Pole beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are the climbing form of the common snap bean: frost-tender, warm-season, nitrogen-fixing legumes grown for their tender immature pods. Unlike the self-supporting bush type, they are twining vines that need a sturdy trellis, teepee, or fence 6 to 8 feet tall to climb. That vertical habit is the payoff: a single planting flowers and sets pods progressively over many weeks, bearing more from the same ground than a bush planting and continuing right up to frost, so you pick regularly rather than facing one concentrated glut. Direct-sown into warm soil after the last frost, they reach a first pickable crop in about 60 to 70 days.

beginner: Beans are ready when the pods are firm and crisp and snap cleanly, before you can see the seeds bulging inside. Pick every two or three days all season. On pole beans, picking often is what keeps new beans coming, so do not let old pods sit on the vine.
seasoned: Pick when pods are firm, crisp, and snap cleanly, before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod wall. Pole beans bear over a long season, so work the vines every two to three days: regular picking keeps the plant flowering and setting new pods, while pods left to mature signal it to slow down.
